title: From Self-Crafted to Engineered Prompts: Student Evaluations of AI-Generated Feedback in Introductory Physics
extended_summary:
This paper examines how introductory physics students evaluate AI-generated feedback produced from different kinds of prompts. The central question is whether students prefer feedback generated from their own self-written prompts, from prompts using foundational prompt-engineering techniques, or from prompts that combine prompt-engineering techniques with principles of effective feedback. The study is motivated by the growing use of generative AI for personalized feedback in large-enrollment STEM courses and by the need to understand how prompt design shapes students’ experiences with AI-supported learning.

The intervention consisted of an extra-credit activity in which students solved a physics problem about the physical significance of the slope of a graph of gravitational potential energy versus distance from a planet’s center. After writing a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning response, students used an AI platform to obtain feedback in three ways: first with a self-crafted prompt (Feedback A), then with a provided prompt incorporating foundational prompt-engineering techniques (Feedback B), and finally with a provided prompt that added effective-feedback principles such as identifying the correct answer, discussing strengths and gaps, and suggesting improvement steps (Feedback C). Students then ranked the usefulness of the three feedback outputs and explained their choices.

The study was conducted with students in a large-enrollment introductory physics course at Purdue University, a midwestern R1 university in the United States. Of 2,044 enrolled students in Spring 2025, 1,235 responded to the Qualtrics-based extra-credit activity. The analysis focused primarily on descriptive trends in students’ rankings of the three feedback types, with brief use of representative qualitative comments to illustrate why students preferred certain versions.

The main conclusion is that students strongly preferred feedback generated from structured prompts over feedback generated from their own prompts. Feedback C, which combined prompt engineering with effective-feedback principles, was most often ranked first (61.4%), while self-crafted-prompt feedback A was most often ranked last (61.2%). The authors argue that these findings support integrating AI literacy and prompt engineering into introductory courses and suggest that AI feedback design should draw more explicitly on established theories of effective feedback. At the same time, they note that the most popular feedback type also produced polarized reactions, and they acknowledge limitations including reliance on one institution, self-reported usefulness rankings, and lack of data on which AI models students used.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI chatbot/LLM used to generate feedback on student work from user prompts; no specific platform or model was recorded for the study tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Students in an introductory physics course used any AI platform of their choice to generate feedback on their written CER arguments using three prompt types: self-crafted prompts, structured prompts with prompt-engineering features, and structured prompts with prompt-engineering plus effective-feedback principles. The study examined students' preference rankings among the resulting feedback versions.

findings.finding_summary: Among 1,235 respondents, students overwhelmingly preferred AI-generated feedback produced from structured prompts over feedback from self-crafted prompts. As first-choice rankings, 61.4% selected Feedback C (prompt engineering + effective-feedback principles), 29.7% selected Feedback B (prompt engineering only), and 8.9% selected Feedback A (self-crafted prompt), meaning 91.1% preferred structured-prompt feedback as their top choice.
findings.measure: Student rankings of usefulness of three AI-generated feedback versions

findings.finding_summary: The most popular feedback type, Feedback C, also elicited polarized reactions rather than broad moderate acceptance. While 61.7% of students ranked C as their top choice, 30.2% ranked it as their least preferred option, and only 8.7% ranked it second.
findings.measure: Distribution of first-, second-, and last-place rankings for Feedback C

findings.finding_summary: Feedback generated from students' self-crafted prompts was least preferred overall. Across 1,235 responses, Feedback A was chosen as the top choice by only 8.9% of students and was ranked least preferred by 61.2% of students.
findings.measure: Student preference rankings for self-crafted-prompt feedback

findings.finding_summary: Second-choice patterns depended strongly on students' first-choice selection rather than showing a single consensus backup option. Of students who ranked A first, about two-thirds ranked C second; among those who ranked B first, about 90% ranked A second; and among those who ranked C first, 95.5% ranked B second and 4.5% ranked A second.
findings.measure: Conditional second-choice rankings given first-choice feedback preference

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical primary study with a large sample, but it measures student preferences/rankings rather than causal learning outcomes and does not control or record the specific AI model used. The design is descriptive survey/activity-based rather than RCT or strong quasi-experiment.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong preference differences for structured prompting, but no standardized learning gains or effect sizes are provided. Impact on student outcomes is therefore suggestive but unclear.
